claims.text: A DNN potential can be trained using high-temperature ab initio configurations from both crystalline and liquid states.
An extensive high-temperature ab initio liquid dataset can provide the proposed DNN reference.
The DNN training dataset will include transitional configurations from liquid and coexisting solid states.
The DNN potential can replace the standard EAM reference in TOR-TILD free-energy integration.
The proposed method applies to equimolar or near-equimolar multicomponent refractory high-entropy alloys.
Equimolar Nb-Ni-Ti-Zr-Co is an example alloy within the proposed scope.
The applicable temperature interval is 0.95Tm to 1.05Tm.
Sampling in the specified temperature interval will adequately cover both liquid and coexisting solid states.
The DNN inherently incorporates high-dimensional many-body and angular-dependent interactions present in ab initio liquid configurations.
The DNN provides a comprehensive mapping of the vibrational and configurational covariance network.
Training directly on ab initio forces and energies over a wide configuration space enables the DNN to represent liquid configurations.
The DNN captures many-body, directional, and anharmonic interactions characteristic of the liquid state.
Improved representation of liquid interactions increases phase-space overlap between the DNN reference and the ab initio target.
Increased reference-target phase-space overlap reduces thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
Traditional EAM references fail to represent many high-dimensional configurations of the ab initio liquid.
The DNN reference will produce a twofold to fourfold reduction in free-energy discrepancy or path mismatch relative to EAM references.
Analogous improvements in elemental and binary systems support the predicted twofold to fourfold reduction.
Insufficient configurational coverage in the training dataset can lead to extrapolation errors.
The benchmark will compare DNN-reference and EAM-reference TOR-TILD calculations against ab initio free-energy results for the same high-entropy alloys.
Failure to achieve at least a statistically significant twofold reduction in path mismatch, or deviation beyond established ab initio uncertainty bounds, will falsify the hypothesis.
